observations.text: In Ezek.14.7 'consult' carries the nuance of hypocritical or corrupted inquiry -- the idolater comes to a prophet to consult God while harboring idols in his heart; the impact is that the surface act of seeking is emptied of sincerity, contrasting sharply with the sincere seeking of Isa.55.6 and 2Chr.1.5.

Other M-codes in Ezek.14.7 (M01 sojourn, M64 separates, M47 heart, M15 putting, M77 stumbling block, M56 iniquity, M43 prophet, M22 answer) surround the consulting act but are not positively related to it: darash here is corrupted by co-present idolatry (M77/M56) rather than harmonizing with them -- the seeking is nullified by what accompanies it, a distinct vantage from any prior finding.

disposition.reason: a co-occurrence note: the M-codes in Eze 14:7 listed, with no link drawn

observations.text: In Ezek.14.7, H1875 is the role-T3 operation: the idolater ('any one', party) initiates consulting, directed toward God via a prophet (parties), though the act is compromised by the idolater's simultaneous devotion to idols.

disposition.reason: an operation note: who initiates the consulting in Eze 14:7, with no inner-being content beyond the idol claim

observations.text: Isa.31.1 and Ezek.14.7 both use 'consult' of illegitimate or compromised inquiry -- Isa.31.1 negates true consultation of the Lord in favor of trust in horses/chariots, while Ezek.14.7 depicts an idolater hypocritically approaching a prophet to consult God while harboring idols in his heart. Both instances show darash's consultation-sense corrupted or withheld by competing loyalties.

Seeking takes hold rightly under conditions of wholeheartedness and sincerity: 'set your mind and heart to seek' (1Chr.22.19), 'with all their heart and with all their soul' (2Chr.15.12), and freedom from co-present idolatry -- in Ezek.14.7 the presence of idols in the heart is what disqualifies otherwise-outward consultation. Genuine seeking requires an undivided heart free from rival objects of devotion.

Seeking is blocked or nullified when the heart harbors idols or a stumbling block of iniquity even while outwardly consulting God -- Ezek.14.3, 14.7 explicitly describe men who 'have taken their idols into their hearts' yet 'come to a prophet to consult me' -- God declares he will not let himself be consulted (or will answer in judgment) in such cases; similarly pride (Ps.10.4 'in the pride of his face') suppresses seeking altogether.

The person whose outward act of inquiry does not take hold rightly is inwardly divided: Ezek.14.3-7 describes them as having 'taken their idols into their hearts' and 'put the stumbling block of their iniquity before their face' -- the inner-being state is one of divided loyalty and self-deception, performing the religious gesture of consultation while the heart remains given to a rival object of devotion.

Uptake of a sought answer from another (a prophet, an oracle) is blocked when the inquirer's heart harbors rival loyalties -- Ezek.14.3-7 shows that idols hidden in the heart nullify the legitimacy of the consultation even though the outward act of inquiry is performed; genuine uptake requires the wholehearted disposition seen elsewhere (2Chr.15.12).

The person who inquires but does not genuinely take up what is sought (as in Ezek.14.3-7) is inwardly divided, harboring 'idols... into their heart' and 'the stumbling block of their iniquity before their face' -- an inner-being state of duplicity, where the outward gesture of consultation masks an unyielded heart.

The pattern of engagement shows heart/soul faculties (mind, will, affection) consistently engaged when seeking is genuine (1Chr.22.19 'set your mind and heart', 2Chr.15.12 'with all their heart and with all their soul'), while purely external/ritual engagement without heart involvement is exposed as illegitimate (Ezek.14.3-7) -- indicating the characteristic's nature is fundamentally a volitional-relational act requiring the engagement of the inner faculties, not a mechanical or merely verbal performance.

At its edge, seeking excludes casual, passive, or half-hearted attention -- it resists mere outward performance without inner devotion (Ezek.14.3-7's idol-hearted consulters are the negative exemplar), and it excludes self-sufficiency/pride that renders inquiry unnecessary (Ps.10.4).

Holiness rules with little inner act: priests are to "abstain from the holy things of the people of Israel, which they dedicate to me, so that they do not profane my holy name" (Lev 22:2); "Thus you shall keep the people of Israel separate from their uncleanness, lest they die in their uncleanness by defiling my tabernacle" (Lev 15:31); "Aaron was set apart to dedicate the most holy things" (1Ch 23:13).
observations.meaning: The word names the keeping of holy things and the separating from uncleanness; no inner act is stated.

observations.text: Among the vowed gifts, a person dedicates what is his own: "When a man dedicates his house as a holy gift to the Lord, the priest shall value it as either good or bad" (Lev 27:14); part of his land, "the valuation shall be in proportion to its seed" (27:16), from or after the jubilee (27:17-18); a field he has bought (27:22). The gift can be taken back at a cost: "if the donor wishes to redeem his house, he shall add a fifth" (27:15; 27:19). If it is not redeemed, "it shall not be redeemed anymore" (27:20).
observations.meaning: Dedicating is a person giving what is his own to the Lord, and the gift is measured by another, can be bought back at a cost, and can be lost for good.

observations.text: What is already the Lord's cannot be given as one's own: "a firstborn of animals, which as a firstborn belongs to the Lord, no man may dedicate; whether ox or sheep, it is the Lord's" (Lev 27:26). Where it is commanded, the dedication is set beside a remembered redemption: "Consecrate to me all the firstborn ... is mine" (Exo 13:2), then "Remember this day in which you came out from Egypt" (13:3); "All the firstborn males ... you shall dedicate to the Lord your God" (Deu 15:19), after "you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the Lord your God redeemed you" (15:15).
observations.meaning: The giving has a limit: what belongs to the Lord is not the giver's to offer, and the commanded dedication answers a redemption remembered.

observations.text: The same giving can be turned to an idol. Micah's mother: "I dedicate the silver to the Lord from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a metal image" (Judg 17:3), in days when "Everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (17:6). Israel "came to Baal-peor and consecrated themselves to the thing of shame, and became detestable like the thing they loved" (Hos 9:10), after "Like grapes in the wilderness, I found Israel". And one "who separates himself from me, taking his idols into his heart" (Eze 14:7), whose heart God means to "lay hold of" (14:5).
observations.meaning: Giving oneself or one's goods can go to an idol in the Lord's name; a person becomes like what he gives himself to and loves, and separating from God is done with idols taken into the heart.

observations.text: Kings and leaders give back the spoil of victory: "These also King David dedicated to the Lord, together with the silver and gold that he dedicated from all the nations he subdued" (2Sa 8:11; 1Ch 18:11), in a passage that ends "the Lord gave victory to David wherever he went" (2Sa 8:14). "From spoil won in battles they dedicated gifts for the maintenance of the house of the Lord" (1Ch 26:27); and what "Samuel the seer and Saul the son of Kish and Abner the son of Ner and Joab the son of Zeruiah had dedicated" (26:28).
observations.meaning: What was won is given back to the Lord who gave the victory, for his house.

observations.text: "Jehoash king of Judah took all the sacred gifts that Jehoshaphat and Jehoram and Ahaziah his fathers, the kings of Judah, had dedicated, and his own sacred gifts ... and sent these to Hazael king of Syria. Then Hazael went away from Jerusalem" (2Ki 12:18), when Hazael "set his face to go up against Jerusalem" (12:17).
observations.meaning: What was given to God, by the fathers and by the king himself, is taken back to buy off a threat.

observations.text: "Behold, I am about to build a house for the name of the Lord my God and dedicate it to him" (2Ch 2:4), after "Solomon purposed to build a temple" (2:1), and with "But who is able to build him a house, since heaven, even highest heaven, cannot contain him? Who am I to build a house for him, except as a place to make offerings before him?" (2:6).
observations.meaning: The house is dedicated inside a purpose, and the one who dedicates it asks who he is to do it.

observations.text: Giving in abundance and with joy: "the people of Israel gave in abundance" (2Ch 31:5) and brought "the tithe of the dedicated things that had been dedicated to the Lord their God" (31:6), and when Hezekiah "saw the heaps, they blessed the Lord and his people Israel" (31:8). In Nehemiah "they set apart that which was for the Levites" (Neh 12:47), where "God had made them rejoice with great joy" (12:43).
observations.meaning: The setting apart of gifts is done in abundance and joy, and is answered with blessing.

observations.text: "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations" (Jer 1:5). Jeremiah answers, "Ah, Lord God! Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth" (1:6), and is told, "Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you" (1:8).
observations.meaning: God's dedicating of a person comes before the person knows or wills; the person's answer is a shrinking that God meets with a sending and a presence.

observations.text: "Should I weep and abstain in the fifth month, as I have done for so many years?" (Zec 7:3). God answers with the aim: "When you fasted and mourned in the fifth month and in the seventh, for these seventy years, was it for me that you fasted?" (7:5), "do you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?" (7:6).
observations.meaning: Abstaining is judged by whom it was for, not by its long keeping.

claims.text: Idols are taken "into their hearts" (Eze 14:3–7); the heart "goes after" idols (Eze 20:16); a "spirit of whoredom" leads astray (Hos 4:12) (dep §2.1i, §2.3c)

tell.part: idols taken into their hearts; a spirit of whoredom leads astray
